tagline: A one-page letter from the elder to a chosen lady and her children, urging love that walks in God's commands and a door closed to teachers who deny Christ came in the flesh.
overview:
Second John is, by word count, the second shortest book in the Bible after Third John, thirteen verses that would fit on a single sheet of papyrus. It comes from a writer who calls himself simply “The elder” and is addressed to “the chosen lady and her children”. The elder is glad to hear that some of her children are walking in the truth. He reminds her of the commandment they have had from the beginning, that we love one another, and he defines that love as walking according to God's commands.

Then comes the warning that gives the letter its urgency. Many deceivers have gone out into the world who refuse to confess the coming of Jesus Christ in the flesh. The lady and her household must not lose what has been worked for, and they must not give such teachers a welcome or a platform. The letter closes with the hope of a visit face to face.

Small as it is, Second John shows how the concerns of First John played out in the ordinary life of a house church: who gets welcomed, who gets hosted, and how love and truth are held together when a community's doors are open to travelers.
author: The writer identifies himself only as the elder (Greek presbyteros, which can mean an older man or a church leader). Early Christian tradition identified him with John the apostle, author of the Gospel and of First John, and the vocabulary and themes of this letter (truth, love, abiding, the commandment from the beginning, the antichrist, Christ come in the flesh) match First John so closely that almost all scholars assign the three letters to the same author or circle. Whether the elder is the apostle himself or another leader named John, sometimes identified with the John the elder mentioned by Papias in the early second century, is debated. The title suggests a senior figure whose authority was recognized across several congregations without needing further explanation.
date: Like First John, the letter is usually dated late in the first century, around AD 85 to 100. Its concerns, especially the deceivers who deny Christ's coming in the flesh, match those of First John, and the two letters were probably written close in time. Some scholars think Second John came first, as a brief warning later expanded; most think First John was written first or at about the same time.
setting:
The church met in a household, and the letter concerns the running of that household. Early Christian mission depended on hospitality: traveling teachers, prophets, and missionaries moved between towns and relied on believers to house and feed them. That system spread the gospel quickly, but it also spread false teaching, because anyone could arrive claiming to speak for Christ. The deceivers of verse 7 belong to the same movement as the secessionists of 1 John 2:19, people who had left the fellowship and were now traveling with a teaching that denied the full humanity of Jesus, very likely an early form of docetism, the belief that the divine Christ only seemed to have a body.

Who the chosen lady is remains open. Many interpreters take her as a figure for a local church, with her children as its members and her elect sister (verse 13) as the church where the elder is. Others think she was a real Christian woman, perhaps a patron who hosted a church in her home. The Greek word kyria, lady, was also used as a personal name, and a few have suggested reading it that way.
purpose: The elder writes to encourage a congregation that is walking in the truth, to remind it of the command to love, and above all to warn it against giving hospitality and support to the traveling teachers who deny that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh. He wants the church to keep what it has received rather than running ahead into a new teaching that leaves Christ behind (verse 9).
story: Second John belongs to the last decades of the first century, when the church had spread across the Roman world and the generation of eyewitnesses was passing. It stands with First and Third John as a window into the churches connected with the apostle John in the province of Asia. The same Christ who, in John's Gospel, became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14) is here the dividing line in the church's life: to remain in his teaching is to have both the Father and the Son. Third John, which follows, shows the other side of the hospitality question, a church leader refusing to welcome faithful missionaries.
christ: The letter's center is the confession that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh. For the elder, the incarnation is not a detail to be adjusted but the heart of the faith: God's Son truly became human. Denying it is the mark of the deceiver and the antichrist (verse 7). Whoever remains in the teaching about Christ has both the Father and the Son (verse 9). The letter also links truth and love in Christ: grace, mercy, and peace come from the Father and from Jesus Christ, the Son of the Father, in truth and love (verse 3).
reading: Read Second John with First John open beside it, since the short letter assumes the argument of the longer one. Notice how often the word truth appears; it is not a set of propositions only but a reality that abides in believers and in which they walk. The instruction not to receive or greet a false teacher (verses 10-11) is often misread as permission for general rudeness or for shunning anyone who disagrees. In context it concerns traveling teachers who deny the incarnation and who would use a church's hospitality as a base for their teaching. The elder's concern is not private disagreement but public sponsorship of a message that empties the gospel.

structure.title: Greeting in truth and love
structure.summary: The elder greets the chosen lady and her children, whom he loves in the truth, with grace, mercy, and peace from the Father and the Son.

structure.title: Walking in truth and love
structure.summary: He rejoices that some of her children walk in the truth and reminds her of the old commandment that we love one another, which means walking in God's commands.

structure.title: Deceivers and the doctrine of Christ
structure.summary: Many deceivers deny Jesus Christ come in the flesh. The church must hold to the teaching of Christ and not welcome or support those who bring another teaching.

structure.title: Closing: hope of a visit
structure.summary: The elder has more to say but hopes to speak face to face, and he sends greetings from the children of the elect sister.

themes.title: Truth
themes.body: The word appears five times in the first four verses. Truth is something believers know, something that abides in them and will be with them forever, and something they walk in. It is finally bound to the person of Christ, and so it cannot be separated from what one believes about him.

themes.title: Love as obedience
themes.body: The elder defines love by action: this is love, that we walk according to his commandments (verse 6). Love is not a feeling set against God's commands but the life those commands describe. It is also the old command, heard from the beginning, not a new discovery.

themes.title: Christ come in the flesh
themes.body: The test of true teaching is the incarnation. Those who deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh have gone beyond the teaching of Christ and do not have God. The letter shows how central the full humanity of Jesus was to the earliest church.

themes.title: Hospitality and discernment
themes.body: The church's open door was one of its great strengths. The elder does not close it; he asks the church to discern whom it sends out with its blessing. Welcome is a form of partnership, and the church must not partner with a message that denies Christ.

keyChapters.why: The whole letter: truth and love held together, and the warning against teachers who deny that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh.

parts.body:
2 John is one of the shortest books in the Bible: thirteen verses, short enough to fit on a single sheet of papyrus. It can be read aloud in about two minutes. It comes from a writer who calls himself simply “The elder”, and it is sent to ‘the chosen lady and her children’.

It does three things. First, it rejoices. The elder has found ‘some of your children walking in the truth’ (verse 4). Second, it reminds. The command they have had from the beginning is ‘that we love one another’ (verse 5), and love means walking in God's commands. Third, it warns. “For many deceivers have gone out into the world, refusing to confess the coming of Jesus Christ in the flesh” (verse 7). The church must hold to the teaching of Christ, and must not give such teachers a welcome and a platform.

Small as it is, 2 John shows how the concerns of 1 John played out in the life of one house church. Who do we welcome? Whom do we send on with our blessing? How do love and truth stay together when a church's doors are open to travellers?

The letter is easily misread, especially its instruction not to receive a false teacher into the house (verses 10-11). These notes set out what it meant in its setting, and what it does not mean.

The writer gives no name. He calls himself ‘the elder’. The Greek word presbuteros can mean an older man or a leader in the church. Here it seems to be a title that needed no explaining: a senior figure whose authority was known across more than one congregation.

Early Christian tradition identified him with John the apostle, the writer long held to stand behind John's Gospel and 1 John. The words and themes of this letter are very close to 1 John's: truth, love, remaining, the command from the beginning, the antichrist, Christ come in the flesh. So almost all scholars think the three letters come from the same writer or the same circle.

Which John is a real question. Papias, a bishop early in the second century, named the apostle John and also a man he called ‘the elder John’, and the historian Eusebius later read him as speaking of two different men. Some scholars think the writer of 2 John was this elder, a leader of the churches of Asia who was not the apostle. Others hold that the apostle, as an old man, called himself ‘the elder’. Others speak of a circle of teachers shaped by the disciple whom Jesus loved.

What is known: the writer was a respected older leader, close in thought and word to 1 John, who expected his letters to be received. What is not known for certain: whether he was the apostle. These notes do not choose. The church received the letter more slowly than 1 John. In the early 300s Eusebius listed 2 and 3 John among the books that were disputed but widely known, and the Syriac churches long read a New Testament without them. In the end they were received across the church.

Who is the lady? The letter does not say plainly, and readers have taken her in two main ways, both with ancient and modern defenders.

Many take her as a picture of a local church. Her ‘children’ are its members, and her ‘elect sister’ (verse 13) is the church where the elder is. They point out that the elder speaks of ‘some of your children’ as if of a congregation, and that the New Testament can picture God's people as a woman: a mother (Galatians 4:26) or a bride (Revelation 21:2).

Others think she was a real Christian woman, perhaps the head of a household who hosted a church in her home. Lydia opened her house to Paul (Acts 16:15), and a church met in Nympha's house (Colossians 4:15). The Greek word for ‘lady’, kuria, was also used as a personal name, and a few readers have suggested ‘Kyria’ as her name.

These notes do not choose. On either reading, the letter is written to a household of faith, and its warnings and its love are for a whole church.

Like 1 John, the letter is usually dated late in the first century, around AD 85 to 100. The two were probably written close together. Most scholars think 1 John came first or at about the same time; some think 2 John came first.

The setting is a house church in a world of travel. The early church spread through hospitality. Teachers, prophets and missionaries moved from town to town and relied on believers to give them a bed, meals and supplies for the next stage. Inns were few and often had a poor name. That way of travelling spread the gospel quickly. It also spread false teaching, because anyone could arrive claiming to speak for Christ.

The deceivers of verse 7 belong to the same movement as those who ‘went out from us’ in 1 John 2:19. They had left the fellowship and were now on the road with a teaching that denied that Jesus Christ came in the flesh, very likely an early form of the belief that the divine Christ only seemed to have a body. Verse 9 calls them people who ‘run ahead’, which suggests they presented their teaching as a more advanced faith, beyond what the church had first received.

The letter follows the pattern of an ordinary letter of its day: sender, readers, greeting, body, and goodbye.

Greeting in truth and love (verses 1-3). The elder to the chosen lady and her children, whom he loves ‘in the truth’. Grace, mercy and peace from the Father and the Son.

Walking in truth and love (verses 4-6). Joy that some walk in the truth. The old command to love one another, and love as walking in God's commands.

Deceivers, and the teaching of Christ (verses 7-11). Many deceivers deny Jesus Christ come in the flesh. Watch yourselves. Remain in the teaching of Christ. Do not welcome those who bring another teaching.

Goodbye (verses 12-13). The elder would rather come and speak face to face. Greetings from the children of the elect sister.

Notice how often ‘truth’ comes: five times in the first four verses. And notice that love comes first in the body of the letter, before the warning.

Some people care most about truth and grow hard. Others care most about love and grow vague. 2 John will not let the two be separated.

The elder loves the lady and her children ‘in the truth’ (verse 1). He loves them because of ‘the truth that abides in us and will be with us forever’ (verse 2). Grace, mercy and peace come ‘in truth and love’ (verse 3). Truth here is not only correct statements. It is God's reality, shown in Christ, that lives in believers and that they walk in.

Then he defines love. “And this is love, that we walk according to His commandments” (verse 6). And the command, in turn, is to walk in love. The two make a circle. Love is not a feeling set against God's commands, and the commands are not cold rules set against love.

That matters for the warning that follows. The elder's warning against false teachers comes from love, not from suspicion. He wants the church to keep what it has. And his love is not a door through which anything may come in.

“For many deceivers have gone out into the world, refusing to confess the coming of Jesus Christ in the flesh. Any such person is the deceiver and the antichrist” (verse 7).

As in 1 John, the word ‘antichrist’ is used of teachers who deny the truth about Jesus. The test is the same: did Jesus Christ truly come in the flesh? For the elder, the incarnation is not a detail to be adjusted. It is the heart of the faith. A Christ who only seemed human could not truly die for anyone.

Over the centuries Christians have often named someone of their own day as the antichrist, or tied the figure to an emperor, a pope, a sultan or a dictator. Such identifications have been made many times. These notes make none. They identify the antichrist of John's letters with no living person, office, church, nation, leader or movement. In 2 John the word describes travelling teachers who denied that Jesus Christ came in the flesh.

Then the elder speaks of running ahead. “Anyone who runs ahead without remaining in the teaching of Christ does not have God” (verse 9). The deceivers offered something new and more advanced. The elder says that going beyond Christ is not progress. It is losing God. ‘Whoever remains in His teaching has both the Father and the Son.’

‘The teaching of Christ’ may mean the teaching about Christ, or the teaching Christ himself gave. Both fit, and both come to the same thing.

parts.h: ‘Do not receive him into your home’
parts.body:
“If anyone comes to you but does not bring this teaching, do not receive him into your home or even greet him. Whoever greets such a person shares in his evil deeds” (verses 10-11). These verses have troubled many readers, and they have sometimes been used to justify cutting off anyone who disagrees.

In their setting their reach is narrow. The house was where the church met. To receive a travelling teacher into the house church was to give him a platform in that congregation and a kind of endorsement. The ‘greeting’ the elder has in mind was most likely the formal welcome and blessing given to a guest teacher, which signalled fellowship and support. The teachers in view denied that Jesus Christ came in the flesh, and they came looking for hospitality as a base for spreading that teaching. To welcome them in that way would be to share in their work.

Christians apply the principle in different ways. Some apply it to any teacher who denies central Christian truth, such as the deity or the humanity of Christ. Others stress that it is about a church's public sponsorship of a teacher, not ordinary courtesy to individuals. Few think it forbids kindness to unbelievers, conversation with doubters, or hospitality to those who differ on smaller questions.

So these verses are not a licence to shun family members, neighbours, or people of other faiths. Jesus ate with tax collectors and sinners. Believers are to be friends, neighbours, coworkers and good citizens with people of every faith and none. Nothing here gives anyone a reason to look down on unbelievers. The same letter that gives this warning commands love.

A word to anyone who has been hurt by a church's discipline, or shunned by a church or a family. What happened to you may have been wrong, and it is not wrong to grieve it. “The LORD is near to the brokenhearted” (Psalm 34:18). If this still weighs on you, please talk with someone you trust, a pastor, a friend or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

The letter is short, but it says a great deal about Jesus. Grace, mercy and peace come ‘from God the Father and from Jesus Christ, the Son of the Father’ (verse 3). The Son stands beside the Father as the source of every good gift. He is not one teacher among many.

Above all, the letter insists that Jesus Christ came ‘in the flesh’. That is the dividing line. The Son of God truly became human, lived a human life and died a human death. The church would later confess it in the Nicene Creed: he ‘came down from heaven’ and ‘was made man’. 2 John is one of the places that confession comes from.

And the letter shows that what we believe about Jesus decides whether we have God: “Whoever remains in His teaching has both the Father and the Son” (verse 9).

2 John does not quote the Old Testament, but its words come from there.

Walking in the truth is the psalms' language: “I have chosen the way of truth; I have set Your ordinances before me” (Psalm 119:30).

The command ‘from the beginning’ goes back to the law: “love your neighbor as yourself” (Leviticus 19:18).

The warning against deceivers echoes the law's warning against false prophets, even ones who did signs: “you must not listen to the words of that prophet or dreamer” (Deuteronomy 13:3). Jeremiah said of the false prophets of his day, “They speak visions from their own minds, not from the mouth of the LORD” (Jeremiah 23:16).

And the welcome of travellers is as old as Abraham, who ran to meet three strangers at his tent and said, “please do not pass your servant by” (Genesis 18:3). 2 John does not cancel that welcome. It asks the church to tell the difference between a guest and a deceiver.

It is not a licence to shun family, neighbours or people of other faiths. Its warning is about a church giving a platform to teachers who deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh.

It is not a call to be rude to everyone who disagrees. It is about the welcome and blessing given to a travelling teacher, not ordinary courtesy.

It is not a warrant to call anyone today ‘the antichrist’. It uses the word for teachers who denied Christ's coming in the flesh, and these notes name no one.

And it is not a letter that sets truth against love. It holds them together from its first line to its last.

Read it with 1 John open beside it. The short letter assumes the longer one's teaching, and it shows that teaching at work in one household.

Read it aloud. It takes about two minutes. Count how often ‘truth’ and ‘love’ come, and notice how they are joined.

Read verses 10-11 in their setting: a house church, a travelling teacher, a request for a bed and a blessing. Then ask what the same care would look like in your own church, without turning it into a reason to shut people out.

Read it beside 3 John, its twin. In 2 John the elder warns a church not to welcome teachers who deny Christ. In 3 John he rebukes a leader who will not welcome teachers who serve Christ. Together they show a church learning to tell the difference.

The notes on the chapter go through it passage by passage in plain words.

hard.line: ‘The chosen lady and her children’: a church, or a woman who led one?
‘This is love, that we walk according to His commandments’.
‘The deceiver and the antichrist’: what the letter means, and why these notes name no one.
‘Anyone who runs ahead’: going beyond the teaching of Christ.
‘Do not receive him into your home’: what it meant, and what it does not mean.

words.line: Greek presbuteros, an older man or a church leader. The writer's title (1:1).
Greek kuria, ‘lady’. A church, or a woman who led one; kuria may also be a name (1:1).
Greek alētheia, God's reality shown in Christ, which abides in believers (1:1-4).
Greek agapē, defined as walking in God's commands (1:5-6).
Greek planos, one who leads others astray (1:7).
One who opposes Christ or puts a false Christ in his place; here, teachers who deny he came in the flesh (1:7).
Greek didachē. ‘The teaching of Christ’: about Christ, or given by him (1:9-10).
To go beyond the teaching of Christ, as if to a higher faith (1:9).

timeline.what: Jesus gives the new command: ‘Love one another’ (John 13:34).
The Romans destroy Jerusalem and its temple.

Papias names the apostle John and also ‘the elder John’.
Eusebius lists 2 and 3 John among the books disputed but widely known.
Athanasius counts the twenty-seven books of the New Testament.

places.name: Ephesus
places.line: The letter names no place. Early tradition places John's last years here, in the Roman province of Asia, and the church has long linked these letters with John there.

teaching.mapNote: 2 John names no place on earth. It does not say where the elder was, or where the lady and her children lived. Early tradition places John's last years at Ephesus, in the Roman province of Asia, so the map shows Ephesus alone.
